title: Fort Jefferson, Clark's fort on Chickasaw ground
summary: In April 1780 George Rogers Clark planted Fort Jefferson and the village of Clarksville below the mouth of the Ohio on Chickasaw land he never bought. A Chickasaw siege that August destroyed the corn, and Virginia gave up the post on June 8, 1781.
bodyMarkdown:
[George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) reached the mouth of the Ohio on [April 19, 1780](https://filsonhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/publicationpdfs/71-3-2_George-Rogers-Clarks-Fort-Jefferson-1780-1781_Carstens-Kenneth-C..pdf), and his Illinois Battalion began a stockade in what is now Ballard County. Virginia called it Fort Jefferson.

## A fort for a charter

In 1777 Gov. [Patrick Henry](/people/#patrick-henry) [proposed a post at the mouth of the Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jefferson_%28Kentucky%29) to protect trade with Spanish Louisiana. In January 1780 Gov. [Thomas Jefferson](/people/#thomas-jefferson) approved it, to hold Virginia's chartered claim to the Mississippi by possession, to guard against a British invasion from the west, and to cut off the arms Britain sent its Indian allies. A civilian town, Clarksville, grew beside the fort. Its families were to farm for themselves and the garrison, since Virginia could send no supplies.

Jefferson attached one condition. The land had to be bought from its Native owners, whom he called Cherokee; the ground was Chickasaw hunting land. Clark [never bought it and never asked their consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jefferson_%28Kentucky%29). Many historians see that choice as the moment the fort was doomed.

## Who lived there

Clark's surviving vouchers and musters [name 551 people](https://filsonhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/publicationpdfs/71-3-2_George-Rogers-Clarks-Fort-Jefferson-1780-1781_Carstens-Kenneth-C..pdf) at the post. They included 267 Virginia state soldiers, 46 Clarksville militiamen and 41 families. At least 100 to 150 people were there at any time, and 65 Kaskaskia people came and went, hunting and fighting beside the garrison.

## Two attacks

Before daybreak on July 17, 1780, Chickasaw warriors fired into the village and attacked the blockhouse for about two and a half hours. Two militiamen died. The commandant, Capt. Robert George, wrote that the town was nearly out of food, with "not one bushel of corn in store."

The siege began on Sunday, August 27. About 150 Chickasaw and two British provincial soldiers surrounded the post. Their commander, John Whitehead of the West Florida provincials, called out at dark that he had come to spare the women and children. The next morning [James Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Colbert_%28trader%29), a trader who lived among the Chickasaw, came under a flag instead.

He said the Chickasaw were angry that Virginians had settled on their land. As Colbert turned away, shots from one of the houses, fired against George's orders, wounded him.

The attackers left on the morning of the 30th. They killed the last cattle and sheep and ruined the corn, more than 1,100 bushels by the garrison's count. Four men of a hunting party were killed and one was captured, and an enslaved woman was shot near the houses.

## Abandoned

Many families left that fall, soldiers deserted, and Virginia could not keep the post supplied. On [June 8, 1781](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jefferson_%28Kentucky%29), the garrison withdrew to Fort Nelson at Louisville. The next year four Chickasaw chiefs wrote that the Americans had built a fort "in our hunting grounds without our permission, and at that location, you suffered most from us."

## Kentucky today

The post stood in what is now [Ballard County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jefferson_%28Kentucky%29), and the map shows this story at county level. [Edward Worthington](/stories/edward-worthington-at-worthingtons-fort/), one of Clark's captains, also served here.
